frames.caption: Ten people, ten heights in centimetres, all example values. Each dot is one sample, and the letter x names a sample, so yours is x = 173 cm.
Count the heights in bins and the pile shows its shape. The mean is the average height, and the variance is the average squared distance from that mean.
Drag μ to slide the bell and σ to widen it. The score adds the log of the bell's height over each of the 10 dots, so a bell that stands tall over every dot scores best.
Call the best bell p(x). Its height is measured per centimetre, so it is a density, telling how thickly heights pile up near x, and never a chance on its own.
The chance of landing in a range is the area under p over that range. A narrow strip has area close to height times width, so one exact height has area zero.
Likelihood multiplies p at every sample, so one badly covered dot drags the whole product down. Taking the log turns the product of ten into a sum of ten.
Slide μ and σ until the score stops rising. The top sits where μ is the average height and σ² the average squared distance, the same two numbers the pile gave.
Score only your own 173 cm and every narrower bell scores higher, so the best fit is a spike of zero width. That is why fitting needs all ten heights.
Sweep from the far left, keeping a running total of the area under p. Call the running total F(x); it climbs from 0 to 1.
Pick a number u between 0 and 1, read across to the curve F and down to the height axis. The height you land on is F⁻¹(u), one sample from the bell.
Feed in many evenly spread random u's and the heights pile up in the bell's shape. All the randomness lives in u, and F⁻¹ is a fixed rule.
A 128 × 128 colour photo stores a red, a green and a blue number for each pixel. Line them up and the photo is one point with 49,152 coordinates, as your height was a point with one.
Each training photo is one sample from a distribution nobody can see, written p(x | dog). Plot any two pixels and the four dogs are four points, as the ten heights were ten dots.
In this four-pixel world only two images exist. Draw each pixel on its own and most results never occur; draw them in order, each given the last, and every result is real.
Drawing in order needs the chance of each pixel value given every earlier pixel, which is a table over every possible image. Count its entries as the image grows.
F⁻¹ is a fixed rule, so the same u always gives the same height and the randomness lives in u. A generator does the same with many numbers, turning a random noise image into a picture.
Fix one training photo and call it x₀. Its noisy copies scatter around √ᾱₜ·x₀, the mean for this one photo, with spread √(1 − ᾱₜ), where ᾱₜ is Step 4's kept share.
When sampling, nobody hands you x₀. Each training height gets a weight for how well it explains the noisy value, and the best guess of x₀ is their weighted average.
Start from pure noise at step 99. Each step guesses x₀, moves part of the way toward the guess and adds a little fresh noise, and every chain ends on a height.
Run the same steps on four dog photos, starting from a pure-noise image. At step 99 the guess is the average of all four dogs, and it sharpens into one dog as t falls.
With the exact best guess the sampler can only return training heights, so the data is everything it knows. A smoother guess, such as a fitted bell, returns new heights in between.

Each weight in the guess is Bayes' theorem: prior times likelihood, divided by the total. The prior is the chance of each height before seeing noise, and the likelihood is how well it explains the noisy value.
Five assumptions carry the whole chain from heights to a dog. Click one to jump to the frame where it does its work.
Swap a convnet for a transformer and the loss and the sampler stay the same. The network is a fixed function, and what its design adds is a preference for which functions are easy to learn.
Each rung changes one thing from the rung below. Teach upward one change at a time, and check each rung on numbers you can drag.
